slides.title: Chronic myeloid leukaemia: key features
bullets: Chronic myeloid leukaemia is the main disease of the chronic myelocytic leukaemia group; marrow cells at first resemble normal cells but differ by carrying the Philadelphia (Ph′) chromosome.
For this leukaemia the genetic factor — a chromosome change — is named most clearly as the cause.
Neutrophilic leukocytosis rises gradually in the blood, the differential shifts toward promyelocytes and myelocytes, and an eosinophil–basophil association appears in the leukocyte formula.

slides.title: Chronic myeloid leukaemia: key features
bullets: The spleen enlarges greatly; in later stages it may rupture (sudden severe pain on the left, signs of acute peritonitis, shock, acute post-haemorrhagic anaemia).
The liver and lymph nodes enlarge; haemorrhagic syndrome and thrombocytopenia occur.

slides.title: Blast crisis and differential diagnosis
bullets: In later stages the patient’s condition worsens quickly: fever, weakness; many blast cells appear in the blood and the leukocyte formula comes to resemble acute leukaemia — blast crisis; chronic myeloid leukaemia turns into acute leukaemia.
Differential diagnosis: leukaemoid reaction (signs of an underlying disease, no metaplasia or anaplasia, passes after treatment).
Osteomyelosclerosis also has leukocytosis and an enlarged spleen, but the marrow is fibrotic and lacks features typical of leukaemia.

slides.title: Blast crisis and differential diagnosis
bullets: Cytochemistry: alkaline phosphatase (phosphomonoesterase I) activity in mature neutrophils is lowered in chronic myeloid leukaemia and raised in a leukaemoid reaction.
In acute myeloblastic leukaemia the blasts are myeloblasts that react positively in cytochemical tests such as peroxidase and chloroacetate esterase.

slides.title: Blood picture more characteristic of chronic myeloid leukemia:
options: hyperleukocytosis, granulocytosis with left shift down to myelocytes

slides.title: Chronic myeloid leukemia. Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture?
bullets: 1. CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm; in ~90–95% of patients t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome, the BCR::ABL1 fusion protein (mainly p210) – a constitutively active tyrosine kinase.

2. Peripheral blood (chronic phase): marked leukocytosis, granulocytes of all maturation stages (many myelocytes and segmented forms – "two-peak" distribution), basophilia and eosinophilia, blasts <2%, platelets often increased.
3. Bone marrow: markedly hypercellular, hyperplasia of the granulocytic lineage, small megakaryocytes; Ph+ cytogenetics.

slides.title: Chronic myeloid leukemia. Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture?
bullets: 4. Phases: chronic → accelerated (increase in blasts and basophils) → blast crisis (myeloid or lymphoid).
5. Confirming the diagnosis: cytogenetics or FISH (t(9;22)), RT-PCR (BCR::ABL1); monitoring treatment – quantitative RT-PCR (molecular response).
6. Difference from a leukemoid reaction: basophilia, BCR::ABL1 positivity, clonality.
